note: Documented cases found by web search on 22 October 2026. Each claim is what the cited source reports. Where sources disagree, the case says so. A record may cite a case from this pool only; any other claim must be written as an inference from the model's principle.

cases.years: From the Sui period (581 to 618), or from the Han; ended 1905
cases.claim: A South China Morning Post feature places the roots of the system in the Sui period (581 to 618), when subject-based examinations replaced hereditary privilege and recommendation, and testing became the standard route for staffing the bureaucracy, with the aim of rewarding ability over favouritism or inherited status. The Tang added local schools to prepare candidates, and the chin-shih examination on the Confucian Classics became the main route into upper officialdom. Qing-era modernisation ended the system in 1905. An online encyclopaedia (secondary) dates its introduction to the Han (206 BCE to 220 CE).
cases.source: South China Morning Post, feature article on the imperial examinations and the gaokao (undated)
cases.caveat: A newspaper feature, not a historical study, read from a search summary without opening the page. The start date is disputed: the encyclopaedia gives the Han and the newspaper the Sui. The Tang detail and the 1905 end date are not tied to this page in the summary.

cases.case: Sweden's parliamentary ombudsman and its spread
cases.claim: Sweden's Instrument of Government of 1809 set up a parliamentary ombudsman as an independent check on the executive. An earlier Supreme Ombudsman post, set up in 1713 under the absolute monarch Charles XII, carried the title Chancellor of Justice by 1719, and that office still operates. Finland's parliamentary ombudsman dates to 1919 and was modelled on Sweden's. Sources disagree on Denmark: one gives 1952 and two give 1955. By 2001, national-level ombudsman offices existed in roughly 110 countries.
cases.source: varuh-rs.si, English web page on the origin of ombudsman institutions in the world (undated)
cases.caveat: Read from a search summary; the page was not opened. The summary does not say which linked page gives the Finland, Denmark and 110-country points. The 1713 precedent rests on one summary line.

cases.case: The Pendleton Act and the end of federal patronage hiring
cases.claim: Patronage hiring gave federal jobs to political backers until 1883. After President Garfield's assassination in 1881 by a frustrated job-seeker, the Pendleton Act was passed in January 1883. It tied federal hiring to merit and competitive examinations, barred firing or demoting covered workers for political reasons, barred compelled political donations, and set up a Civil Service Commission to enforce these rules. Coverage began at close to a tenth of federal jobs. Partisan turnover in the White House from 1884 to 1896 moved most federal jobs under the merit system. A 1981 court case, Luévano v. Campbell, moved most federal hiring away from one uniform examination (PACE).
cases.source: US National Archives, Milestone Documents page on the Pendleton Act (undated)
cases.caveat: Read from a search summary; the page was not opened, and the summary draws on several reference sites without saying which gives each point. The near-a-tenth coverage figure is undated, and the results give no year-by-year coverage figures after 1883.

cases.case: The Soviet nomenklatura: party control of appointments
cases.claim: Key posts in the USSR and other Eastern Bloc states fell under the nomenklatura, which ran on two registers: one of posts that party authorities filled, and another of eligible candidates. Cadre control moved through bodies including Uchraspred (1919 to 1924), the Orgburo and the Secretariat. Lenin's stated yardsticks for placement included dependability, ideological stance, skill and managerial aptitude. Ties of patronage bound appointees to their sponsors. Accounts of the end differ: an online encyclopaedia (secondary) describes late-1980s signals of a planned cut in appointment power, while a National Chengchi University thesis speaks of the system's abolition under Gorbachev.
cases.source: GlobalSecurity web page on the CPSU nomenklatura (undated)
cases.caveat: Read from a search summary; the page was not opened, and the summary does not say which linked page gives each point. The end date is disputed, as the claim states. Items on Estonian party lists are left out because the summary does not tie them to a page.

cases.case: Germany's 1933 law removing officials for political or racial reasons
cases.claim: The Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service took effect on 7 April 1933, about two months after Hitler's rise to power, and sought to rebuild a 'national' bureaucracy by removing selected classes of career officials. Officials with a Jewish parent or grandparent, labelled 'non-Aryan', faced immediate retirement. Officials tied to opposition groups, or deemed disloyal, risked removal without cause. Rulings by top Reich or state agencies could not be appealed. Exemptions for front-line First World War veterans were added at Hindenburg's insistence and later whittled away. Tallies for 1933 alone count some 2,000 civil servants and 700 academics among those removed.
cases.source: University of Oregon, course page on the 1933 law (undated)
cases.caveat: Read from a search summary; the page was not opened, and the statute text was not checked. The 2,000 civil servant and 700 academic tallies have no named source in the summary, so they may come from another page. The veterans' exemption is a single summary line.

cases.case: Hong Kong's Independent Commission Against Corruption after the Godber affair
cases.years: 1973 to 1975; enabling ordinance in force from 15 February 1974
cases.claim: Peter Godber, the subject of a police corruption probe, left Hong Kong on 8 June 1973 using a special airport permit issued to police. Public anger followed, and the colonial administration under Governor Murray MacLehose set up the Independent Commission Against Corruption. Its enabling ordinance took effect on 15 February 1974. The commission superseded the police Anti-Corruption Office and operates independently of the police and the civil service. Godber was taken into custody in England in April 1974, sent back to Hong Kong in January 1975, and convicted of corruption in February 1975.
cases.source: Independent Commission Against Corruption (Hong Kong), history web page (undated)
cases.caveat: Read from a search summary; the history page was not opened, and the summary does not tie each date to it. Accounts differ on what started the probe (a 1973 bank inquiry in one account, a transfer of 12,000 Canadian dollars in the commission's case history) and on Godber's holdings (above 4.3 million, 3.4 million and more than 4 million Hong Kong dollars). Early complaint and prosecution counts come from a secondary website that attributes them to Robert Klitgaard, so they are left out.

cases.case: New Zealand's State Sector Act 1988 and fixed-term chief executive contracts
cases.claim: The 1988 reform replaced open-ended tenure for state-services chief executives with fixed terms capped at five years. A 2019 commentary says contracts in practice ran three to five years, with total tenure often reaching about eight years. It argues that short terms leave top officials more exposed to political pressure and encourage short-term thinking, and that political leaders used gaps in the Act to gain more sway over appointments.
cases.source: Newsroom (New Zealand news site), commentary 'A largely unnoticed power grab', 2019 (dated 20 November 2019 by its web address)
cases.caveat: An opinion piece, read from a search summary without opening the page; its contract-length figures are the author's reading, not primary data. The results say little about performance agreements. The Act's text (sections 35 to 43 of a 2013 reprint) appeared in the results but was not opened.

cases.case: Japan's first recommended pay cut for national civil servants
cases.claim: In 2002 the National Personnel Authority recommended, for the first time, a cut in the monthly pay of national public employees, averaging 2.03 per cent. The article reports that monthly pay, including base pay and dependent allowances, had run 7,770 yen above private-sector levels.
cases.source: English archive article of a Japanese labour-policy institute on the first recommended pay cut (2002 archive, year taken from the page address)
cases.caveat: Read from a search summary; the article was not opened. The results hold no later year-by-year pay series. Press reports on the 2026 pay round are undated and are not used.
